## Plain English Summary

::: lang-en
Multiple sclerosis (MS) often affects women during their childbearing
years. When relapses occur during pregnancy, they may be treated with
high-dose glucocorticoids such as methylprednisolone. While this
treatment can be important for the mother, much less is known about
whether exposure before birth may have longer-term effects on the child.

The MS-Children project examines whether prenatal exposure to
methylprednisolone is linked to later differences in children's
development. We compare children whose mothers received this treatment
during pregnancy with children of mothers with MS who were not exposed
to the medication before birth.

Our aim is not only to look at general development, but also at
specific areas that may be relevant for later health and functioning.
These include thinking and memory, behaviour, stress regulation, and
brain development. To do this, the project combines cognitive
assessments with methods such as brain imaging, measures of stress
hormones, and other biological markers.

The study is based on the idea that experiences before birth can
influence later development. By investigating this question in a
clinical population, we hope to better understand the long-term safety
of an important treatment used during pregnancy.

Overall, the project aims to provide evidence that can support more
informed medical decision-making for pregnant women with MS and
their families.
:::

::: lang-de
Multiple Sklerose (MS) betrifft häufig Frauen im gebärfähigen Alter.
Wenn während der Schwangerschaft Schübe auftreten, kann eine
Behandlung mit hochdosierten Glukokortikoiden wie Methylprednisolon
notwendig sein. Während diese Therapie für die Mutter wichtig sein
kann, ist bislang wenig darüber bekannt, ob eine Exposition vor der
Geburt längerfristige Auswirkungen auf das Kind haben könnte.

Das Projekt MS-Kinder untersucht, ob eine vorgeburtliche Exposition
gegenüber Methylprednisolon mit späteren Unterschieden in der
Entwicklung von Kindern zusammenhängt. Wir vergleichen Kinder, deren
Mütter diese Behandlung während der Schwangerschaft erhalten haben,
mit Kindern von Müttern mit MS, die vor der Geburt nicht dem
Medikament ausgesetzt waren.

Unser Ziel ist es nicht nur, die allgemeine Entwicklung zu
untersuchen, sondern auch spezifische Bereiche, die für die spätere
Gesundheit und das Funktionieren relevant sein könnten. Dazu gehören
Denken und Gedächtnis, Verhalten, Stressregulation und
Gehirnentwicklung. Hierfür kombiniert das Projekt kognitive
Assessments mit Methoden wie Bildgebung des Gehirns, Messungen von
Stresshormonen und anderen biologischen Markern.

Die Studie basiert auf der Überlegung, dass Erfahrungen vor der
Geburt die spätere Entwicklung beeinflussen können. Indem wir diese
Frage in einer klinischen Population untersuchen, hoffen wir, die
Langzeitsicherheit einer wichtigen Behandlung in der Schwangerschaft
besser zu verstehen.

Insgesamt zielt das Projekt darauf ab, Erkenntnisse zu liefern, die
eine fundiertere medizinische Entscheidungsfindung für schwangere
Frauen mit MS und ihre Familien unterstützen können.
:::

## For Researchers

**Status:** [Ongoing]{.status-ongoing}

**My role:** Doctoral candidate

**Responsibilities:** Data collection across both study centres
(Jena and Bochum); scoring and evaluation of neuropsychological
assessments; database maintenance; personalised feedback to
participating families; data analysis; manuscript drafting and
editing across multiple planned outputs; international conference
presentations.

**Design:**
Cross-sectional, two-centre study. School-aged children (mean age
~9–10 years) with prenatal exposure to methylprednisolone due to
maternal MS relapse treatment were compared with a non-exposed
reference group, all born to mothers with MS. Participants were
primarily identified via the German MS and Pregnancy Registry.
Primary outcome: global cognitive ability (standardised IQ test).
Secondary outcomes: attention, behaviour, motor performance,
electrocortical activity, and structural brain development assessed
via high-resolution MRI including voxel-based and surface-based
morphometry and a machine learning–based brain age framework.

**Key findings (primary outcome paper):**
- No significant difference in global IQ between MP-exposed
(n = 30; IQ: 103.0) and non-exposed children (n = 30; IQ: 101.5)
- No group differences in neuropsychological secondary outcomes
or electrocortical parameters after correction for multiple
comparisons
- MRI analyses revealed no differences in grey matter volume,
cortical thickness, gyrification, or brain age
- Findings suggest that MP exposure, predominantly in the second
trimester at the doses used, does not measurably affect
neurodevelopment, though the study was not powered to detect
subtle dose-response effects

**Trial registration:**
[NCT04832269](https://clinicaltrials.gov/ct2/show/NCT04832269?id=ZKSJ0130)

**Funding:**
Grant for Multiple Sclerosis Innovation 2020 (Merck Healthcare KGaA);
BMFTR (CEPRE; funding reference: 01GR2305A).

**Publications:**
- Kozik V et al. (2025). Multiple Sclerosis Relapse Treatment
During Pregnancy and Offspring Functional and Structural
Neurodevelopment. *Neurology.*
[DOI: 10.1212/WNL.0000000000214217](https://doi.org/10.1212/WNL.0000000000214217)
- Kozik V et al. (2022). Protocol for a Cross-Sectional Study:
Effects of a Multiple Sclerosis Relapse Therapy With
Methylprednisolone on Offspring Neurocognitive Development and
Behavior (MS-Children). *Frontiers in Neurology.*
[DOI: 10.3389/fneur.2022.830057](https://doi.org/10.3389/fneur.2022.830057)
